d: Tracks stockpile chemistry (CaO, SiO₂, MgO), material movement, and reclaiming patterns across quarry stockpiles in real time.
Flags likely chemistry deviation (LSF drift) in the reclaimed material before it enters the raw mill.
Guides quarry teams on blending and reclaiming sequence/locations to homogenise chemistry and stabilise raw mix feed.
p: No real-time visibility into stockpile chemistry, so quality teams operate blind to in-pile variability.
Random/sequential reclaiming (rather than chemistry-led) creates chemistry fluctuations entering the plant.
Resulting raw mix instability increases corrective material usage and downstream kiln upsets.

d: Monitors crusher load, feed size/hardness, motor current, and operating conditions in real time.
Estimates specific power consumption (SPC) and throughput for the current feed and operating settings.
Recommends optimal feed rate and operating parameters to maximise throughput while minimising SPC.
p: High crusher specific power consumption due to sub-optimal operating settings.
Frequent idle running and stoppages reduce effective utilisation.
Variable throughput caused by inconsistent feed size and operator-driven settings.

d: Analyses raw material chemistry, online process data (PGNAA/XRF), and laboratory measurements across limestone, clay and correctives.
Models the resulting clinker chemistry (LSF, SM, AM) and kiln feed uniformity for a given proportioning combination.
Recommends the optimal raw material proportions to hit target clinker chemistry and stable kiln operation.
p: Natural variability in limestone, clay, and corrective materials causes fluctuations in LSF, SM, AM and kiln feed quality.
Manual proportioning based on delayed lab feedback results in unstable kiln operation and higher SHC.
Frequent chemistry deviations increase corrective material consumption and operator interventions.

d: Tracks raw mill process parameters – throughput, mill DP, roller pressure, separator speed, motor current – in real time.
Predicts raw meal Blaine and residue (fineness), ahead of laboratory results.
Recommends mill and separator setpoints to hold target fineness while minimising grinding energy.
p: Raw meal Blaine is typically measured via periodic lab testing, causing delayed process corrections.
Under- or over-grinding adversely affects calcination efficiency, kiln stability and clinker quality.
Operators struggle to balance throughput, fineness and power consumption, leading to inconsistent mill performance.

d: Continuously monitors mill loading, grinding/hydraulic pressure, separator speed, fan power, vibration, and feed material hardness/moisture.
Identifies the specific power consumption (SPC) and maximum sustainable throughput achievable for the current operating window.
Recommends the optimal feed rate, grinding pressure and separator settings to jointly minimise SPC and maximise throughput within safe stability limits.
p: Raw mills are among the largest power consumers in a plant, and inefficient operation significantly increases production cost.
Mills often run below maximum sustainable capacity due to conservative operator settings, while pushing feed rate without understanding constraints risks high vibration, trips and poor fineness.
Variations in raw material hardness, moisture and operating conditions cause inconsistent mill performance, higher kWh/ton, and increased reject rates.

d: Continuously monitors kiln operating data – burning zone temperature, torque, feed rate, speed, secondary air temperature, and gas analysis (NOx, O₂, CO).
Predicts the burning zone state (stable/unstable) and emerging risk of free lime excursions or ring formation.
Recommends proactive adjustments to feed rate, fuel, and kiln speed to restore and hold the optimal burning zone.
p: Burning zone instability leads to fluctuations in clinker quality, increased free lime, ring formation, and higher SHC.
Operators rely on manual observation and experience to adjust kiln parameters, resulting in reactive decision-making.
Changes in raw mix, fuel quality, and production rate make it difficult to consistently maintain the optimal burning zone.

d: Analyses kiln thermal and combustion data – feed rate, BZT, torque, secondary/calciner temperature, O₂/CO/NOx, and fuel mix including TSR.
Forecasts the Specific Heat Consumption (SHC) trajectory for the current operating configuration.
Recommends operating parameter adjustments to minimise SHC while holding clinker quality and throughput targets.
p: Kiln SHC is highly influenced by raw mix quality, fuel properties, kiln loading, and combustion efficiency.
Operators rely on experience to adjust kiln parameters, leading to inconsistent thermal performance and excess fuel use.
Even small increases in SHC translate into significant annual fuel cost and higher CO₂ emissions.

d: Uses kiln process parameters, raw mix chemistry, fuel properties (incl. AFR feed rate) and operational data as inputs to a soft sensor.
Predicts clinker Tricalcium Silicate (C₃S) in near real time, ahead of laboratory results.
Flags the process corrections (feed, fuel, kiln speed) needed to bring C₃S back within target before a quality deviation occurs.
p: C₃S is one of the most critical clinker quality parameters, directly influencing strength and grindability.
Laboratory testing introduces delays of 30 minutes to several hours, so operators act without real-time quality feedback.
Variations in raw mix chemistry, fuel ash contribution and burning zone conditions cause unstable C₃S and inconsistent clinker.

d: Continuously monitors cyclone differential pressure, preheater draft, stage-wise temperatures, hot meal chemistry (SO₃, Cl, alkalis) and ID fan load.
Predicts the likelihood and location of cyclone build-up/blockage 30-60 minutes ahead of occurrence.
Triggers early alerts and recommends preventive actions (feed/fuel adjustment, targeted cleaning) at the at-risk cyclone stage before a stoppage occurs.
p: Cyclone build-up and jamming are a leading cause of unplanned kiln stoppages, causing major production losses and safety risk.
Operators typically detect blockages only after abnormal pressure drop or temperature change, leaving little time to react.
Variations in raw meal chemistry, volatile cycles and material flow make blockage hard to predict with conventional monitoring.

d: Continuously evaluates kiln thermal loading – BZT, torque, filling ratio, feed rate, secondary air temperature, and gas composition.
Identifies the degree of excess/conservative thermal loading relative to the actual heat requirement of the process.
Recommends safe reductions in coal feed rate while protecting clinker quality and kiln stability.
p: Operators often run a conservative (higher-than-required) coal feed to avoid instability, causing excess fuel consumption.
Overheating conditions are hard to identify accurately as they depend on multiple interacting parameters.
Without a data-driven approach, excess thermal energy raises fuel cost, refractory stress and NOx emissions.

d: Uses kiln process parameters, raw mix chemistry (LSF, SM, AM), fuel conditions, and burning zone behaviour as inputs to a soft sensor.
Predicts clinker free lime (f-CaO) in near real time, ahead of laboratory results.
Recommends process corrections to avoid both under-burning (high free lime) and over-burning (excess fuel use).
p: Free lime is a critical burnability/performance indicator, but lab measurement is delayed by 30-90 minutes or more.
High free lime indicates under-burning, while excessively low free lime indicates over-burning and wasted fuel.
Variations in raw mix chemistry, burning zone conditions and fuel quality make it hard to consistently hold target free lime.

d: Continuously monitors clinker outlet temperature, secondary/tertiary air temperature, cooler fan power, bed depth, grate speed and DP.
Estimates the cooler's heat-recuperation efficiency and the resulting secondary/tertiary air conditions for the kiln and calciner.
Recommends optimal fan and grate-speed settings to maximise heat recovery and stabilise downstream combustion.
p: Inefficient clinker cooling results in loss of valuable heat, raising SHC and fuel cost.
Poor cooler operation destabilises secondary/tertiary air temperatures, affecting combustion in the kiln and calciner.
Operators rely on experience to adjust fans and grate speeds, causing inconsistent cooling efficiency and excess power use.

d: Continuously assesses kiln shell temperature profile, BZT, torque, feed rate, coating stability and thermal cycling at each kiln location/zone.
Detects abnormal wear patterns and estimates the refractory health index and remaining refractory life by kiln zone/location.
Provides early warnings and recommends operating adjustments and maintenance/replacement timing to extend campaign life and avoid emergency shutdowns.
p: Refractory is one of the most critical and expensive consumables, and unexpected failures cause major losses.
Excessive temperatures, thermal shocks and unstable coating accelerate wear but are hard to detect before visible damage.
Maintenance decisions rely on periodic inspection rather than continuous monitoring, leading to premature replacement or surprise outages.

d: Continuously monitors kiln torque, BZT, filling ratio, volatile cycle chemistry (SO₃, Cl, alkalis), and cyclone DP.
Identifies the risk of ring formation hours to days before it becomes operationally critical.
Recommends adjustments to fuel mix, raw mix chemistry or kiln operation to dissipate the ring risk before a shutdown is required.
p: Rings form from accumulation/sintering of material driven by unstable burning conditions and volatile cycles.
Ring formation restricts material flow, increases torque, destabilises operation, and can force unscheduled shutdown.
Operators typically identify rings only after symptoms appear (rising torque, falling throughput), by which time output is already affected.

uc.t: Vision-Based AFR (Alternative Fuels & Raw Materials) Monitoring
d: Deployed at AFR feed belts and dosing stations feeding the kiln main burner and calciner/precalciner.
Continuously monitors AFR feed belts via 24x7 camera feeds – fuel type (plastics, rubber, biomass, RDF), colour, texture, particle size and oversize/foreign objects.
Classifies the fuel mix in real time and estimates the calorific value of the AFR being fed to the kiln/calciner.
Recommends AFR feed-mix and dosing adjustments to maintain consistent calorific value and combustion stability.
p: AFR composition and calorific value vary widely batch-to-batch, with no continuous visibility into what is actually being fed.
Inconsistent calorific value and oversized particles or foreign objects destabilise combustion and increase equipment wear.
Manual sampling-based quality checks are infrequent and cannot keep pace with continuous AFR feed variability.

d: Tracks grinding process parameters – mill DP, separator speed, motor current, reject rate, clinker hardness and gypsum quality.
Predicts cement fineness (Blaine) and residue, ahead of laboratory results.
Recommends separator and mill setpoint adjustments to hold target Blaine while avoiding over-grinding.
p: Blaine is typically measured via periodic lab testing, delaying corrective action by 30-60 minutes or more.
Variations in clinker hardness, gypsum quality, separator efficiency and mill conditions cause inconsistent fineness and excess power use.
Operators often over-grind to avoid quality risk, increasing SPC and reducing mill throughput.

d: Continuously monitors mill motor power/current, separator speed, grinding pressure (VRM), circulating load, vibration, and clinker/gypsum/additive proportions.
Identifies the specific power consumption (SPC) and maximum achievable throughput (TPH) for the current grinding circuit condition.
Recommends the optimal feed rate, separator speed, and grinding-pressure settings to jointly minimise SPC and maximise throughput at target Blaine.
p: Cement grinding is one of the highest electrical energy consumers in a plant, directly impacting production cost.
Mills are often run conservatively due to quality, vibration, or circulating-load concerns, underutilising available capacity.
Variations in clinker hardness, gypsum proportion, additives and circulating load increase grinding energy and limit throughput without additional CAPEX visibility.

uc.t: Model Digital Plant – IT-OT Integration Platform
d: Integrates process, quality, maintenance, laboratory, ERP (SAP) and energy data from PLC/DCS, historians, LIMS and EMS into a single contextualised data model.
Powers plant-wide AI/analytics models (SHC, quality, reliability, energy) by giving them a single, reliable source of real-time data.
Delivers standardised KPI dashboards, GenAI copilots and root-cause/benchmarking views that guide cross-functional decisions.
p: Critical plant data is distributed across disconnected systems (PLCs, DCS, Historians, LIMS, SAP, EMS), making holistic analysis difficult.
Engineers and management spend significant time manually collecting, reconciling and validating data before decisions can be made.
Lack of integrated data prevents implementation of advanced AI use cases such as kiln optimisation, predictive maintenance and energy optimisation.

d: Continuously monitors camera feeds of personnel across plant operational and hazardous areas.
Detects PPE non-compliance (missing helmet, shoes, jacket, gloves) and unauthorised entry into restricted zones, in real time.
Triggers immediate alerts to supervisors/EHS teams for corrective action and zone-specific safety interventions.
p: Manual monitoring of PPE compliance is inconsistent and cannot provide 24x7 coverage across large cement plants.
Workers may inadvertently enter hazardous areas without mandatory safety gear, increasing accident risk and regulatory exposure.
Safety incidents can lead to injuries, production disruption, legal liability and reputational damage.

d: Covers critical rotating assets across raw mill, kiln, cement mill, crusher, fans, conveyors and utilities (CPP/WHRS), replacing line-specific predictive-maintenance use cases.
Continuously monitors vibration, bearing/gearbox temperature, motor current, lubrication health and operating condition of critical rotating and static assets plant-wide.
Predicts the equipment health index and remaining useful life / failure probability for each monitored asset.
Recommends maintenance timing and spare-part planning based on actual asset condition rather than fixed time intervals.
p: Traditional preventive maintenance is time-based, resulting in unnecessary maintenance or unexpected equipment failures.
Maintenance teams often lack a unified, plant-wide view of equipment health to prioritise interventions.
Spare-part planning is reactive rather than condition-driven, raising inventory and emergency-procurement cost.

d: Deployed across limestone/raw material yard conveyors, coal handling conveyors, clinker transport conveyors, and cement/finished-product handling conveyors.
Continuously monitors conveyor belts via industrial camera feeds – surface condition, tracking/alignment, edge wear, tears and spillage.
Detects developing belt damage and predicts the likelihood of failure (tear, mistracking, edge damage) before it becomes critical.
Generates early-warning alerts for inspection or maintenance action at the specific belt and location flagged, ahead of breakdown.
p: Conveyor belts are critical assets across limestone, raw material, coal, clinker and cement handling, and unexpected failures cause major disruption.
Traditional inspections are manual and periodic, often missing developing issues such as edge damage, tears or mistracking.
Belt failures lead to production losses, material spillage, safety hazards, and costly replacements.

d: Deployed at crusher discharge, raw material stockpile reclaim conveyors, coal mill feed conveyors, and clinker/cement transfer points.
Continuously analyses material images from conveyor belts and transfer points across the material-handling circuit.
Estimates particle size distribution (PSD) and material moisture trend for the feed stream in real time.
Flags feed-rate/process setpoint adjustments needed at the crusher, raw mill, coal mill or cement mill to correct off-spec feed before it impacts the downstream process.
p: Particle size and moisture are typically measured via periodic manual sampling and lab testing, resulting in delayed, reactive corrections.
Variations in limestone fragmentation, clinker size or coal particle distribution reduce crusher efficiency and increase grinding energy.
Excessive material moisture can destabilise mills, reduce throughput, and raise drying energy and specific power consumption.

d: Deployed at crusher inlet conveyors, raw material and coal feed conveyors, and transfer points ahead of crushers and mills.
Continuously scans material on conveyor belts using industrial cameras to spot tramp metal, wood, rock chunks, plastic and other foreign objects.
Detects and classifies foreign objects in real time before they reach the crusher, mill or downstream equipment.
Triggers automatic alerts or belt-trip/diverter actions to remove the foreign object before it causes equipment damage.
p: Tramp metal, oversized rocks and other foreign objects entering crushers and mills cause liner, hammer and roller damage and unplanned stoppages.
Manual visual inspection cannot provide continuous, 24x7 coverage of fast-moving conveyors.
Existing metal detectors often miss non-metallic foreign objects (wood, plastic, large rocks), leaving a detection gap.

d: Deployed on bus bars, joints and terminations inside LT/HT switchgear, MCCs, and key electrical panels across the plant.
Continuously monitors bus bar and joint temperature in real time using wireless IoT temperature sensors.
Detects abnormal heating trends and predicts the risk of a hotspot developing into a loose-connection or insulation failure.
Triggers early alerts to electrical maintenance teams to tighten, clean or replace the affected joint before failure or fire.
p: Loose connections and degrading bus bar joints generate hotspots that can cause electrical fires, equipment damage and unplanned plant trips.
Conventional thermal-imaging inspections are periodic and manual, often missing fast-developing hotspots between inspection rounds.
Wired temperature sensors are costly and impractical to retrofit across the large number of joints and panels in a cement plant.

d: Continuously monitors kiln/cooler exhaust gas temperature, AQC/SP boiler conditions, steam parameters and turbine performance.
Estimates the achievable WHRS power generation for the current kiln load and waste-heat availability.
Recommends operating adjustments across kiln, cooler and WHRS to maximise heat recovery and power generation.
p: WHRS performance varies significantly with kiln load, exhaust gas temperature, cooler operation and process stability.
Operators have limited visibility into the link between kiln process parameters and WHRS power generation, leading to underutilisation.
Inefficient heat recovery increases grid power dependency and reduces overall plant energy efficiency.

uc.t: Net Heat Rate (NHR) Optimization in Captive Power Plant (CPP)
d: Continuously monitors boiler, turbine and auxiliary system data – coal GCV, steam flow/pressure/temperature, turbine load and condenser vacuum.
Identifies the Net Heat Rate (NHR) and root causes of efficiency loss for the current operating configuration.
Recommends corrective actions on combustion, boiler and turbine operation to minimise fuel use per unit of power generated.
p: CPP efficiency deteriorates over time due to sub-optimal combustion, poor boiler performance, turbine inefficiencies and high auxiliary consumption.
Operators often cannot identify root causes of high NHR in real time, leading to increased coal consumption and cost.
Even small increases in NHR translate into substantial annual fuel cost and reduced plant profitability.

d: Consolidates plant-wide electrical and thermal energy consumption by section (raw mill, kiln, cement mill, utilities), tariff structure, and captive/grid/WHRS generation mix.
Forecasts section-wise and plant-level energy demand, maximum demand (MD) excursions, and the cost impact of the current generation/consumption mix.
Recommends optimal load scheduling, power-source dispatch (grid/CPP/WHRS/renewables) and demand-control actions to minimise overall energy cost.
p: Energy consumption and cost data are tracked in silos across sections, with no single real-time, plant-wide view of energy cost drivers.
Maximum demand (MD) penalties and sub-optimal source dispatch (grid vs. CPP vs. WHRS vs. renewables) increase the effective cost per unit of power.
Lack of granular, real-time visibility limits the ability to act before high-cost demand or generation-mix excursions occur.
